prompt: Under the blocklist, the new cache on db port 6379 was open to remote. Why?

choices.text: 6379 is a port that firewalls leave open
choices.why: No port is special; the policy was accept.

choices.text: Everything not named is allowed, and nobody named it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The cache opened the firewall itself
choices.why: Nothing touched the firewall.

choices.text: The database rule on 5432 covered the cache as well, by mistake
choices.why: That rule named 5432 only.

prompt: What is the cost of an allowlist, and why is it the better failure?

choices.text: Something legitimate is refused and somebody complains within the day
choices.why: Right. The blocklist's failure is silent.

choices.text: It is slower, because every packet is compared with every rule
choices.why: Speed is not the trade.

choices.text: It cannot express a rule for the internet
choices.why: The baseline has rules for the internet.

choices.text: Nothing; it has no cost
choices.why: It refuses what nobody listed, legitimate or not.

prompt: Under the blocklist, which of these were open to the internet? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: app:22
choices.why: Nobody listed SSH.
Nobody listed the application.
Started after the list was written.
That one was on the list and blocked.

prompt: What does nft -c -f do?

choices.text: Loads the file and prints a copy of it
choices.why: It loads nothing.

choices.text: Checks the file, changing nothing
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Clears the counters first, then loads
choices.why: That is not what -c means.

choices.text: Compiles the file into a faster form
choices.why: Nothing is compiled for later.

prompt: After nft -f failed on the misspelt file, how many accept lines did the running rule set have?
A file starts with flush ruleset and has an error on line 7. Without atomic loading, what would the firewall be left with?

choices.text: The old rule set, untouched
choices.why: That is what atomic loading gives, not what its absence does.

choices.text: The whole new file, minus line 7
choices.why: Loading stops at the error.

choices.text: A flushed firewall with lines 1 to 6 loaded
choices.why: Right. Neither the old policy nor the new.

choices.text: No rules and a policy of drop on every chain
choices.why: The chain definitions come from lines that may not have run.

prompt: A script of fifty iptables commands fails at the twentieth. What state is the firewall in?
hint: iptables applies one rule per command.

choices.text: Unchanged, as with nft -f
choices.why: Each command applied on its own.

choices.text: Nineteen new rules applied, the rest missing
choices.why: Right. iptables-restore exists for this.

choices.text: Every rule applied except the twentieth one that failed
choices.why: The script stops at the failure unless told otherwise.

choices.text: Rolled back automatically to the rules saved at boot
choices.why: Nothing saved them.

prompt: Put the safe way to change a remote firewall in order.
hint: The way back is scheduled before the change.
items: save the working rule set, starting with flush ruleset
schedule a job that reloads it in a few minutes
test from where you are, then cancel the job
trap: Scheduling after the change is too late if the change locks you out.

prompt: The rollback restored the saved output of nft list ruleset, and the count of accept lines came back as 13 instead of 11. Why?
hint: What does the listing not start with?

choices.text: The counters were saved as extra rules
choices.why: Counters are part of rules, not new ones.

choices.text: The background job ran twice
choices.why: It ran once; rollback.log has one line.

choices.text: The listing has no flush ruleset, so it merged with the loaded rules
choices.why: Right. The tighter chain's two rules appeared twice.

choices.text: nft -f doubles rules loaded from a listing
choices.why: It adds what the file says; the file said too little.

prompt: A saved rule set replaces the running one only if its first line is ___ ruleset.
hint: Two words, the first is a verb.

prompt: Which chain protects fw itself, rather than the zones behind it?

choices.text: input
choices.why: Right. Packets addressed to fw.

choices.text: forward
choices.why: That is traffic crossing fw.

choices.text: output
choices.why: That is traffic fw makes.

choices.text: postrouting
choices.why: That is where NAT happens.

prompt: Match each ICMP message to what breaks without it.

pairs.right: path MTU discovery, and large transfers stall

prompt: From admin, probe fw:22 said refused. What does refused show here?

choices.text: The input chain rejected it
choices.why: The chain drops; it sends nothing back.

choices.text: admin is not in the management range that input allows
The rule let it in, and fw runs no SSH server
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: SSH is blocked on the loopback
choices.why: admin reaches eth4, not lo.

prompt: Why does the log rule carry limit rate 5/second?
hint: Who controls how many packets are dropped?

choices.text: nflog accepts at most five packets a second from the kernel
choices.why: The limit is a choice, not nflog's.

choices.text: Otherwise the disk fills with anybody's dropped packets
choices.why: Right. The log would become the attack.

choices.text: It slows the attacker down to five packets a second, at most
choices.why: It limits logging, not the traffic.

choices.text: tcpdump reads no faster than that
choices.why: It reads far faster.

prompt: Of the three drops logged, which deserves a person's attention first?
hint: Which is the internet's background noise?

choices.text: 203.0.113.50 to the database
choices.why: The internet tries doors all day.

choices.text: 203.0.113.50 to SSH on app
choices.why: Also the internet's background noise.
Right. A LAN machine reaching for a service it was never given.

choices.text: None; drops mean the firewall worked
choices.why: It worked, and one of them still says something.

prompt: Why is the log rule the last rule of the chain?
hint: What would it record anywhere else?

choices.text: Placed earlier, it logs traffic later rules allow
choices.why: Right. Last means about to be dropped.

choices.text: nftables refuses a log rule placed anywhere else in a chain
choices.why: It accepts it anywhere.

choices.text: The policy reads the last rule as its own log target
choices.why: The policy has no log target.

choices.text: So its rate limit applies to every rule
choices.why: A rule's limit applies to that rule.

prompt: On a network with IPv6, what does a firewall with only a table ip do to IPv6 packets?
hint: A table ip handles one family.

choices.text: Drops them, since no rule accepts them
choices.why: No chain of that family exists to drop them.

choices.text: Nothing: they pass unfiltered
choices.why: Right. An invisible policy of accept.

choices.text: Translates them to IPv4 first
choices.why: Nothing translates them.

choices.text: Applies the same rules automatically
choices.why: That is what the inet family does, not ip.

prompt: After 192.168.99.11 was added to the admins set, what changed in the rules?

choices.text: A new rule was added for the new address
choices.why: No rule was added.

choices.text: Every rule was reloaded from the file on disk, with the address in it
choices.why: Only the set changed.

choices.text: No rule changed; every rule naming the set now includes it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The set's comment was updated
choices.why: The comment stayed.

prompt: On Friday evening an administrator must tighten fw's input chain over SSH from admin. Which plan is safe?
hint: Check, save, schedule, load, test, confirm.

choices.text: Load the new file, then save a backup
choices.why: If the load locks you out, the backup does nothing.

choices.text: Edit the running rules one by one with nft add
choices.why: Each step applies alone, and the file drifts.

choices.text: Check with nft -c, save with flush ruleset, schedule the rollback, load, test, cancel
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Set the input policy to accept while working
choices.why: That opens fw to every zone.

prompt: Which habits make a rule set safer for the next person? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A comment on every accept naming the decision
choices.why: The rule cannot say why.

choices.text: The file in version control, changed by commits
choices.why: A history with reasons.

choices.text: Named sets for groups used in several rules
choices.why: One change, applied everywhere.

choices.text: Editing the running rules directly, then exporting
choices.why: The file should be the source, not a copy.

prompt: An office turns IPv6 on for its staff LAN and keeps its table ip rule set. What have they opened?
hint: The rule set filters one family.

choices.text: Nothing, since the policy is drop
choices.why: That policy belongs to the ip family's chains.

choices.text: Every zone, over IPv6, to anything routed
choices.why: Right. Move the tables to inet.

choices.text: Only ICMPv6, which the rule set never names
choices.why: Every IPv6 packet, not only ICMPv6.

choices.text: Nothing new, as IPv6 has its own firewall built in
choices.why: IPv6 has no built-in firewall.
